title: How to Break ADHD Task Paralysis (When You're Frozen)

scenes.text: You know exactly what you need to do. You've known for three days. And you're still sitting here, scrolling, feeling worse every hour. That's not laziness. It's called task paralysis. And there's a simple way out.

visual.query: person lying on couch scrolling phone

scenes.text: Task paralysis is that frozen feeling when you want to start, but you can't make yourself move. It usually isn't about not caring. Researchers connect it to executive function, the brain skills that help you plan, prioritize, and get started.

People with A D H D often describe a few things that set it off. The task is too big, so there's no clear first step. There are too many tasks, so choosing feels impossible. It's boring, so your brain can't find a reason to begin. Or it feels high stakes, and you're scared of doing it wrong.

items.text: Too big: no clear first step
High stakes: scared to get it wrong

scenes.text: Then the worst part kicks in. The longer you wait, the bigger it feels. You feel guilty, the guilt makes it heavier, and you freeze even harder. Willpower doesn't break that loop. Smaller steps do.

visual.query: stressed woman at desk head in hands

scenes.text: Here's a method you can use right now. Step one. Pick one task. Just one. Step two. Shrink the first step until it feels almost silly. Not clean the kitchen. Put one cup in the sink. Step three. Set a timer for five minutes, and promise yourself you can stop when it rings. Step four. Move your body first. Stand up and walk to where the task happens. Step five. Do the tiny step. Then pick the next one.

steps.text: Do it, then pick the next

scenes.text: Why can this help? A tiny step gives your brain one clear action, so there's less to plan. The timer makes the task feel finite. And once you've started, keeping going is often easier than beginning was. It won't work every single time, and that's okay. Just try again with an even smaller step.
